official_title: Budget stabilization fund. Proposing an amendment to the State Constitution to increase the amount of funds that may be retained in the budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% of general revenue collections, require the legislature to transfer the lesser of $750 million or the amount required to reach 25% of the general revenue collections each year unless certain conditions are met, and allow the legislature to withdraw funds for critical state needs.
plain_summary: Florida's rainy-day savings fund is capped at 10% of yearly general revenue. This raises the cap to 25% and requires a deposit of up to $750 million a year until the fund gets there. It also lets lawmakers spend some savings on a 'critical state need' with a two-thirds vote.
yes_means: The state must deposit up to $750 million a year into its rainy-day fund until it reaches 25% of general revenue, and may spend some on a 'critical state need' with a two-thirds vote.
no_means: The rainy-day fund stays between 5% and 10% of general revenue, with no required $750 million yearly deposit and no 'critical state need' withdrawals.
current_law: Article III, section 19(g) of the Florida Constitution requires a Budget Stabilization Fund of at least 5% and at most 10% of the last completed fiscal year's net general revenue collections. Money may be withdrawn to cover a revenue shortfall or an emergency and must be paid back in five equal yearly installments. Voters created the fund in 1992; it was last tapped in 2008.
fiscal_impact: No Financial Impact Statement: Florida's Financial Impact Estimating Conference writes those only for citizen initiatives, not legislative referrals. Practical effect per Florida TaxWatch: a required transfer of $750 million a year from general revenue into savings until the fund reaches 25%, money that otherwise could be spent, refunded, or cut from taxes. The transfer can be skipped in years the fund is tapped, or once every five years by a two-thirds vote.
pass_threshold: 60% of votes cast on the measure (Florida Constitution, Art. XI, s. 5(e))
confusing_wording_note: This isn't a tax and doesn't change what you pay. 'Unless certain conditions are met' means lawmakers can skip the yearly deposit in some years (for example, once every five years by a two-thirds vote). 'Critical state needs' isn't defined in the amendment; lawmakers can only use it when the fund is above 15%, and can't drop it below 10%.

supporters_case.text: House Speaker Daniel Perez, sponsor Rep. Lawrence McClure (R-Dover) and the Republican Party of Florida say a bigger reserve protects Florida's credit rating and forces the state to spend less so it can weather a recession or a major hurricane without cuts or tax hikes. Florida TaxWatch recommends yes, calling reserves sound fiscal practice.

opponents_case.text: Gov. Ron DeSantis opposes it, calling the plan 'foolish' and arguing extra money should go to tax cuts. Newspaper editorial boards (Orlando Sentinel, Miami Herald, Sun Sentinel, TCPalm) say Florida already holds large reserves, the fund has not been needed since 2008, and a mandatory $750 million a year ties future legislatures' hands and centralizes power in Tallahassee.

official_title: Exemption of tangible personal property on agricultural land from taxation. Proposing an amendment to the State Constitution to exempt tangible personal property habitually located or typically present on land classified as agricultural, used in the production of agricultural products or for agritourism activities, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder of the agricultural land from ad valorem taxation. If approved this amendment would first apply for tax years beginning January 1, 2027.
plain_summary: Ends local property tax on farm equipment and similar property (tractors, irrigation gear, agritourism fixtures) kept on farmland, used for farming or agritourism, and owned by the farmer or the person leasing the land. It starts with the 2027 tax year.
yes_means: Farm equipment and similar property on agricultural land becomes exempt from local property taxes starting in 2027.
no_means: Farm equipment stays taxable as tangible personal property the way it is now (with the existing $25,000 exemption that applies to all businesses).
current_law: Businesses, including farms, pay local ad valorem tax on tangible personal property (equipment, furniture, machinery) above a $25,000 exemption (Art. VII, s. 3(e)). Agricultural land is already assessed at its agricultural-use value under the 'greenbelt' law, but the equipment on it is taxed like any other business's equipment.
fiscal_impact: Local governments and school districts would lose about $31.0 million in FY 2027-28, $32.3 million the second year and $33.6 million the third (state Revenue Estimating Conference figures as reported by Florida TaxWatch and the Tampa Bay Times). Rural counties with lots of farmland feel it most.
pass_threshold: 60% of votes cast on the measure (Florida Constitution, Art. XI, s. 5(e))
confusing_wording_note: 'Tangible personal property' is a legal term for things of value that aren't land or buildings, like equipment. 'Ad valorem' means regular property tax. This doesn't change the tax on farmland itself.

supporters_case.text: Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson, the Florida Farm Bureau Federation and Florida TaxWatch back it, saying farms being 'choked out' by costs need relief on equipment taxes, the tax is expensive to administer and comply with, and the revenue loss is small.

opponents_case.text: Rep. Anna Eskamani (D-Orlando), the lone House vote against putting it on the ballot, worries about lost revenue for rural, less-wealthy counties. The Miami Herald editorial board says big agribusiness, not mom-and-pop farms, would benefit most; the Orlando Sentinel and Sun Sentinel also recommend no.

official_title: Increased homestead exemption; lower cap on increases in non-homestead property assessments. This amendment increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. It requires the Legislature to prescribe a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities, for their respective levies, to increase the homestead exemption up to full assessed value, and allows special districts, subject to referendum approval, to do the same. Persons who are not Florida residents on December 31, 2026, will receive the existing homestead exemption upon qualifying for a homestead exemption, with the increased homestead exemption beginning with the fifth year of exemption, to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution. This amendment reduces the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. This amendment requires counties and municipalities to use property taxes solely for public safety, education and schools, infrastructure, natural resources, bond debt service, retirement benefits for employees, and operations and administration. Other expenditures may be approved by county officers or county or municipal governing bodies unless prohibited by general law, notwithstanding Article VII, Section 9(a) of the Florida Constitution, which allows counties and municipalities to levy property taxes for their respective purposes. This amendment takes effect January 1, 2027.
plain_summary: For your main home, the break on city, county and other non-school property taxes rises from up to $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The yearly cap on assessment increases for other property drops from 10% to 5%. Cities and counties could spend property taxes only on listed purposes. School taxes don't change.
yes_means: Homeowners get a bigger break on non-school property taxes (up to $250,000 by 2028), the cap for other property drops to 5%, and cities and counties may spend property taxes only on listed purposes.
no_means: The homestead break on non-school property taxes stays at up to $50,000, the cap for other property stays at 10%, and there are no new limits on what cities and counties spend property taxes on.
current_law: Homesteads get a $50,000 exemption (the second $25,000 does not apply to school taxes) plus the 3% 'Save Our Homes' cap on yearly assessment increases. Non-homestead property has a 10% yearly assessment cap (non-school levies). Counties and cities may levy property taxes 'for their respective purposes' (Art. VII, s. 9(a)).
fiscal_impact: State Revenue Estimating Conference, as reported by Florida TaxWatch: local government property-tax revenue falls $4.939 billion in 2027 and $8.714 billion in 2028, growing to $11.835 billion by 2031; five-year total $45.837 billion. Example county figures reported by the Tampa Bay Times: Hillsborough loses about $261 million in 2028 and $468 million the next year; Miami-Dade $357 million then $643 million. The amendment gives local governments no replacement revenue.
pass_threshold: 60% of votes cast on the measure (Florida Constitution, Art. XI, s. 5(e))
confusing_wording_note: Three things hide in the long summary. (1) 'For all non-school taxes': your school tax bill doesn't change. (2) People who aren't Florida residents by December 31, 2026 get only the current exemption until their fifth year. The Florida Supreme Court struck down a similar waiting period in the 1980s, which is why the summary says 'to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution.' (3) The cap cut from 10% to 5% is for non-homestead property, so it also helps landlords, second-home owners and businesses.

supporters_case.text: The Republican Party of Florida, Gov. DeSantis (who first proposed the idea) and Florida Realtors say Floridians are being priced out of their homes, that this is the biggest property-tax cut in state history, and that it makes homeownership more attainable while forcing local governments to prioritize core services.

opponents_case.text: The Florida Sheriffs Association, firefighter unions, the Florida League of Cities, the Florida Hospital Association, the Florida Democratic Party, the League of Women Voters of Florida and Florida TaxWatch oppose it, warning of deep cuts to police, fire and basic services. TaxWatch says it 'shifts the burden onto non-homestead property owners' and was 'rushed onto the ballot.'

short_title: Property tax exemptions and assessment limits
